OUTDOOR RECREATION STRATEGY 
Funding of €30,000 per county has been provided by the Department of Rural and 
Community Development and the Gaeltacht (DRCDG) to support the development of an 
Outdoor Recreation Strategy, with a recent additional €10,000 allocated for environmental 
screening and translation into Irish.  
The development of the Outdoor Recreation Strategy will be a key objective for 2026. The 
strategy will align with the national framework Embracing Ireland’s Outdoors and guide the 
strategic enhancement of outdoor amenities across Galway. The strategy will play a key role 
in advancing our recreational development agenda, strengthening our capacity to deliver

high-impact recreational infrastructure and to support communities in accessing and 
enjoying Galway’s natural assets.  It will also assist in identifying projects for delivery under 
the Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS). 
The development of the strategy will be informed by an extensive public consultation 
process to include direct engagement with key stakeholders and the establishment of a 
County Outdoor Recreation Committee. 
The Outdoor Recreation Team are delighted to confirm that the Department of Rural and 
Community Development and the Gaeltacht has approved funding of €245,700 for the 
construction of a 2.5km walkway with low level lighting around the perimeter of the Renville

construction stage).

12 
 
Sustainable, Inclusive and Empowered Communities (2019 – 2024) 
 
This is a whole of government strategy led by the DRCDG, which set out a long-term vision 
for communities in Ireland and a general direction of travel for government policy in relation 
to community development, local development and the community and voluntary sectors 
for the coming years. 
  
The new strategy will look to build upon the structures, achievements and objectives of 
Sustainable, Inclusive and Empowered Communities, to further support the community 
and voluntary sector in Ireland and strengthen the relationship between government and 
the C&V sector at local and national level. It will aim to create a supportive policy, funding 
and institutional environment within which the sector operates, locally and nationally 
It will also provide a high- level framework within which related policies that affect the C&V 
sector will operate. 
  
This strategy is currently in the developmental phase, and as part of this process the 
Department are consulting with stakeholders, including other Government Departments, to 
share their views on key strategic and cross-cutting issues to help shape these strategies for 
this period. 
Building on the work of the Department since its establishment in 2017 and reflecting 
commitments in the new Programme for Government, the DRCDG would be grateful to 
receive your input and views on: 
  
• initiatives/objectives under your organisations remit that should be identified 
and prioritised in this strategy. 
• Any current/planned developments relating to your organisations engagement 
with the Community and Voluntary sector 
  
As a key stakeholder in this process, and should it be desired, the Department are available 
to engage in a bi-lateral discussion on topics that you consider warrant inclusion in this 
strategy.  
 If you would like to provide your views centrally, the department are asking for views to be 
submitted by email to communitypolicy@drcdg.gov.ie.

PRIDE OF PLACE COMPETITION 
Clarinbridge has been named winner of the ‘300 – 1,000 Population’ category at the 2025 
IPB Pride of Place Awards, held on the 7th November at the Strand Hotel in Limerick.   
Nominated by Galway County Council to represent the county in the all-island competition, 
the south Galway village was selected for its exemplary community development efforts.   
The Pride of Place Awards, now in their 23rd year, are organised by Co-operation Ireland 
and sponsored by IPB Insurance.   The programme recognises voluntary groups that 
demonstrate a strong commitment to improving their local areas through collaboration and 
civic engagement. 
 
Established in 1979, the Clarinbridge Tidy Towns group has played a central role in 
enhancing the village’s physical and social environment.   It has been a part of projects 
involving the maintenance of local landmarks such as The Green, Parish Hall, Kilcornan 
Estate, and Cowpark. The village also promotes heritage and environmental care through 
the development of walking trails and green spaces. 
Judges commended Clarinbridge’s partnerships with organisations including the 
Clarinbridge Men’s Shed and SCCUL Sanctuary, as well as its annual events such as 
Clarinbridge Market Day and Halloween on the Green. 
The Marconi Men’s Shed in Clifden also represented Galway County in this year’s 
competition, competing in the ‘Community Wellbeing’ category.   Although not a category 
winner, the group was recognised for its innovative approach to supporting male family 
carers and promoting health and wellbeing in the Connemara region.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION NETWORK (PPN) 
The second PPN plenary meeting for 2025 is scheduled to take place on Wednesday 
November 12th @7pm. This is an online meeting. This will be a FREE gathering and 
networking event for community and voluntary groups from around the County. It will be an 
opportunity for volunteers to pick up useful information for their community and for their 
community groups.   The Public Participation Network (PPN) is a network of over 1300 
community & voluntary groups from all over County Galway. Its main purpose is to act on 
behalf of communities and provide input into local policies and plans at decision making 
committees both within Local Authorities and on other organisations. It is also an 
information sharing platform where PPN registered groups get regular information on topics 
that are of interest to them such as funding schemes, community events and training 
workshops There will be short presentations with a focus on the various departments of 
Galway County Council pertaining to Community Grants & Services, Galway Rural 
Development pertaining to SMART Villages Projects and Campion Insurance regarding 
Community Insurance. The PPN Plenary will provide a great opportunity for volunteers and 
community groups to learn about grants, procurement and community insurance.

CREATIVE IRELAND 
October and November are a hive of activity in Creative Ireland. Over the past few weeks 
there has been a steady stream of projects finishing up as we approach the deadline for 
recoupment. Funding for the Creative Ireland programme is divided into a number of 
categories, including Open Call projects, Culture and Creativity Team projects, and Flagship 
projects. Below are some recently completed examples from the 2025 programme.  
CREATIVE IRELAND OPEN CALL 
Each year we run an Open Call for funding. This year 12 projects out of 59 applications were 
successful. A total of €71,055 was awarded to projects covering every Municipal District. 
Many have been reported on in previous management reports, so below is a rundown of 
the most recently completed projects.  
ATHENRY MUSIC SCHOOL – JOINING OF WORLDS 
Athenry Music School joined the old and the new together with their project ‘Joining of 
Worlds’, wherein the historical setting of Athenry’s Medieval castle was used as the 
backdrop for a pop venue. 
Orchestral arrangements were 
created for modern pop songs 
as audiences of the younger 
and older members of the 
community came together in a 
collaborative celebration of 
music and heritage.  In total 
almost 200 people were 
involved in this project, either 
as performers or audience 
members.  
CREGGS RURAL DEVELOPMENT CLG – CREGGS QUILT 
Creggs Rural Development made their first application to the Creative Ireland Open Call this 
year for a wonderful community project. Over the course of the summer months, a group of 
people came together to create a heritage quilt for Creggs. The project took place every 
Thursday evening from 7.30 to 9 pm. The group 
consisted of people living in the village for many 
years, new residents, people with intellectual 
disabilities, people from Ukraine who came to 
the area following the onset of war, elderly 
people, young people and was a wonderful 
opportunity for people to get to know each 
other. A decision was made to base the design of

PORTUMNA ARTS GROUP – A PATTERN FOR PORTUMNA 
This intergenerational project saw students from Youthreach Portumna work collaboratively 
with senior attendees at the Portumna Day Care Centre to create a piece of mosaic artwork 
which is now on display at the local library. An artist worked with the participants to 
develop a diamond shape which could then be customized and personalized to match the 
tastes of each individual. This project gave participants an opportunity to have a meaningful 
and tangible effect on the aesthetic appeal of their town. Staff at the Day Care Centre 
reported an increase in social skills amongst their senior attendees and students reported a 
strong sense of personal reward.

2025, County Galway was 
impacted by a series of 
significant weather events, 
including prolonged rainfall, 
extensive flooding, high winds, 
coastal surges and wave 
overtopping. These events 
placed sustained pressure on 
the road network, water and 
wastewater operations, 
electricity and 
telecommunications systems 
and several vulnerable coastal 
communities. The cumulative effect of these events required ongoing mobilisation of 
Council resources and inter-agency coordination. 
 
In advance of each event, Galway County Council activated its Severe Weather Assessment 
Teams and convened both Local and Regional Coordination structures. This ensured that all 
relevant agencies had early awareness of the developing conditions and could prepare 
personnel and resources effectively. Depots and outdoor crews were placed on standby, 
with enhanced rostering arrangements introduced for Orange and Red level alerts. The 
Council also implemented its communication plans at an early stage through its 
Communications Unit within Corporate Services, ensuring that timely updates were issued 
to the media, local radio, elected members, and across social media platforms. This 
proactive approach helped to ensure that the organisation, partner agencies, and the wider 
public were well informed in advance of the worst weather conditions. 
 
The Council’s emergency response reflected the varied and significant impacts of each 
storm. In responding to Storm Bert, which affected Connemara and Clifden, Galway County 
Council worked closely with the Fire Service to undertake pumping operations to prevent 
properties in Clifden from flooding, while also managing substantial landslides that occurred 
in the surrounding area. During Storm Éowyn and Storm Darragh, the county experienced 
major tree falls that resulted in widespread disruption to the road transport network. In 
response, the Municipal District offices and outdoor crews carried tree out clearance 
operations, prioritising national primary roads, followed by national secondary and regional 
routes, and finally local roads, in order to restore access in the quickest possible time to 
ensure emergency services access and allow essential travel to resume after the passing of 
each storm event.

90 
 
Following each severe weather event, the Council moved swiftly into the recovery phase by 
reopening roads, removing debris and carrying out temporary or permanent repairs as 
required. After Storm Éowyn, when prolonged and widespread power outages affected 
communities across the county, Galway County Council, supported by the Community Unit, 
worked with community centres to provide community hubs. Throughout the recovery 
period, Galway County Council maintained close coordination with ESB Networks. As part of 
this effort, the Council worked closely with elected members to gather details on hardship 
cases reported by residents who were without power for extended periods. This 
information was relayed to ESB Networks on a regional basis to support the prioritisation of 
power restoration for the most vulnerable and severely impacted households. 
 
While the impacts of severe weather events are often unavoidable, an essential component 
of the Council’s response is the provision of clear and timely communication to the public. 
Effective communication delivers key messages regarding weather forecasts, anticipated 
impacts and safety advice, enabling communities to take appropriate actions in advance of 
and during severe weather. Communication with elected members is equally important, as 
they are closely connected to local communities and play a vital role in relaying information 
and reassurance. Throughout each weather event, Galway County Council, through the 
Communications Unit within Corporate Services, issued regular updates to the media, local 
radio, and social media channels to keep the public informed of evolving conditions and 
potential impacts. Senior representatives of the Council also participated in live radio 
interviews to advise the public on storm impacts, the local authority’s response measures 
and available supports.  
 
The severe weather experienced during the winter of 2024 and into 2025, including three 
Red Weather Warning events, demonstrated the strength and resilience of Galway County 
Council’s emergency management arrangements. Across each event, the Council’s proactive 
preparation ensured that transport links could be reopened rapidly once the immediate 
hazards had passed, allowing communities and essential services to resume activity without 
undue delay. The response was characterised by strong internal coordination across 
multiple departments and units, including the Community Department, Corporate Services, 
Housing, the Fire Service, Rural Water Services, ICT, Roads and Transportation, and the 
Municipal District offices. This whole-of-Council response ensured that the full range of 
expertise and resources within the organisation was utilised effectively to support 
communities. 
 
Galway County Council operated under the Western Regional MEM Steering Group 
including neighbouring local authorities, An Garda Síochána, the HSE’s emergency 
management structures and in partnership with Uisce Éireann and ESB Networks. This 
integrated approach assisted coordinated of public messaging and coordination of our 
operational response throughout each event.

PROPOSED SOLUTIONS 
ESTABLISHING A LIFESCIENCES CAMPUS 
Developing a centralised campus dedicated to lifesciences can provide multifaceted benefits. 
A state-of-the-art facility featuring co-working spaces, specialised labs, can significantly 
reduce startup costs while enhancing operational efficiency. There is a need for a campus that 
allows a company to grow from a start-up to a multinational on the same campus. 
Access is needed to preclinical animal facilities within Ireland and a holistic and streamlined 
clinical research infrastructure. 
  Key infrastructural needs identified include: 
• Community space 
• Wet labs and clean-room facilities 
• Testing and prototyping labs 
• Shared resources and equipment to minimize overhead costs 
• Flexible office spaces accommodating varying company sizes 
• Pre-clinical Animal testing facilities 
• Clinical Research Infrastructure 
• Sterilisation facilities 
• Transportation testing 
  
Lack of housing is a significant issue and needs urgent attention. The campus will only be 
viable and sustainable if the housing issue can be resolved.

among startups in specific fields—such as wound care—will foster shared resources and 
knowledge. 
LEARNING FROM INTERNATIONAL MODELS 
Exploring successful lifesciences hubs around the world (e.g., Denmark, the Netherlands, and 
California) can provide valuable insights into best practices for infrastructure, funding 
facilitation, and talent acquisition. Tailoring these examples to meet the unique needs of 
Galway and the region will be crucial.

Galway and the West of Ireland has an established reputation in lifesciences being 
recognised as a global hub for Medtech, in particular. The opportunity to sustain and build 
on this exists, however, addressing several infrastructural operational challenges will be 
important to realising this. Establishing a dedicated lifesciences campus will provide 
essential resources for startups and scaling companies alike and strengthen the overall 
ecosystem through connectivity, shared knowledge, and operational efficiencies. By aligning 
the needs of the sector with strategic planning and industry engagement, Galway and the 
region can sustain and build on its position of strength.  
There is considerable support for building and enhancing the community collaboration and 
learning that has been initiated by the lifesciences ecosystem and in particular in recent 
times through the MedLink cluster. The activities of the cluster need to be supported,

position to be the ‘go to place’, a central resource and connector for the sector facilitating 
and co-ordinating on many initiatives to support start-ups, SMEs and MNCs collaboratively.

CORRIB ISLAND SURVEY 2005 
The 2025 Corrib Island Survey funded through the Local Biodiversity Action Fund from the 
NPWS has now been completed. This project set out to document the flora of 15 islands in 
Lough Corrib and compare findings with previous surveys from 1974 and 1992. Islands were 
selected based on minimal human interference and historical data availability. Fieldwork 
involved 20 visits over eight days, recording all flowering plants and ferns, supported by 
photographic documentation of habitats and geomorphology. Data were compiled into a 
comprehensive database for analysis. A total of 149 species were recorded across 13 fully 
surveyed islands. Preliminary analysis revealed that tree and shrub species have expanded 
their range, while species of open habitats have declined. Severe impacts from Ash Dieback 
and Storm Éowyn were observed, particularly on large limestone islands where fallen timber 
and dense bramble growth made surveys challenging. The repeated surveys of many islands 
on Lough Corrib has allowed rarely acquired data on extinction and colonization over a 50-
year period to be assembled. 
The project’s legacy lies in its contribution to understanding vegetation change over five 
decades and its enhancement of the conservation value of Lough Corrib’s islands. These 
islands serve as important reference sites in County Galway for natural woodland and fen 
communities, offering opportunities for further studies on fungi, invertebrates, and habitat 
classification.

CONNECTING LANDSCAPES FOR WILDLIFE: A PARTICULAR FOCUS ON THE LESSER 
HORSESHOE BAT IN COUNTY GALWAY 
Biodiversity in Ireland is under pressure, and County Galway is no exception. Habitat loss 
and fragmentation—caused by changing land use—leave wildlife struggling to survive in 
small, isolated patches of woodland and hedgerows. This isolation reduces genetic diversity, 
making species less resilient to change. 
To tackle this, Galway County Council partnered with the Vincent Wildlife Trust to study 
habitat connectivity for the lesser horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus hipposideros), an Annex II 
species of the Habitats Directive. These bats rely on linear features like hedgerows and 
treelines to move safely across the landscape. 
Using advanced modelling tools, the study mapped potential movement routes and 
identified “pinch points” where connectivity is most at risk. Results show that bat 
movement is concentrated along narrow corridors near the N59, with critical areas around 
Ross Lake and Cloghaun. Artificial lighting emerged as a major threat—adding streetlights 
creates barriers, while reducing lighting dramatically improves connectivity. 
This work directly supports actions in the Lesser Horseshoe Bat Species Action Plan, guiding 
Galway County Council to protect ecological corridors, apply best-practice lighting 
standards, and integrate connectivity into planning decisions. These measures are essential 
to prevent further fragmentation and secure a healthy, connected landscape for future 
generations. This study was supported through the Local Biodiversity Action Fund 2025 from 
the NPWS.

DEALING WITH AFTERMATH OF STORM AMY ON 3RD OCTOBER 
Intense rainfall led to a number of landslides and flash floods in the Maum Valley/Partry 
Mountains area after heavy rainfall during the 2nd and 3rd of October. The L-1301 Local 
Primary Road to Finny in the townland of Na Gringeacha suffered when a flash flood 
resulted in a section of road-retaining rock armour and parapet wall being severely 
damaged. This same location suffered extensive damage during Storm Bert in November 
2024, and although the damage wasn’t as severe on this occasion, with the road remaining 
passable, there is significant stabilization works required to try and contain the damage and 
prevent further degradation over the upcoming winter period.  
Another landslide occurred during the night of the 2nd November further to the north along 
the same road, but Council workers worked through extremely poor conditions to reopen 
this road by the afternoon of the 3rd November.

The Gateway to the Corrib initiative is linked to a cycling and tourism route around Lough 
Corrib, primarily focused on Headford and surrounding areas. It aims to connect 
communities on both sides of the lake and promote outdoor recreation and tourism. 
Funding of €18,000 was secured under the Outdoor 
Recreation Infrastructure Scheme for signage along 
the Headford–Kilbeg cycle loop through Claran. This 
includes interpretive and directional signs for cyclists 
and visitors.

businesses. The completed schemes focused on upgrading non-public roads that serve 
multiple homes and agricultural holdings, ensuring safer and more reliable connectivity. This 
achievement reflects ongoing collaboration between Galway County Council, local 
communities, and the Department of Rural and Community Development, and contributes 
to the broader goal of enhancing rural mobility and supporting economic activity in the 
region.

SAFETY WORKS 
Significant progress was achieved in 2025 on road safety improvements within the Tuam 
Municipal District. Key projects included traffic signal upgrades at critical junctions in Tuam, 
aimed at improving traffic flow and reducing collision risk. In addition, safety schemes were 
completed on Weir Road, Milltown Road, and Gilmartin Road, addressing identified collision 
trends and enhancing pedestrian and cyclist safety. These works form part of Galway County 
Council’s commitment to the Regional Road Network Safety Analysis (RR NSA) objectives 
and the national Vision Zero strategy, targeting zero fatalities on Irish roads by 2050. 
Measures implemented include improved signal phasing, enhanced signage, and junction 
layout adjustments to mitigate turning conflicts and improve visibility for all road users.
